title: Trump Demands 20% Hormuz Toll — JMIC Records 4 Transits vs 138 Normal — His Own Officials Called It Illegal
narrative:
President Donald Trump declared on Truth Social on July 14 that the United States would be known as "THE GUARDIAN OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT" and would charge a 20% reimbursement fee on all cargo shipped through the waterway. Trump claimed "oil is flowing like never before" because of U.S. military operations in the region.

The Joint Maritime Information Centre (JMIC) reported only 4 Strait of Hormuz transits on July 12 and 12 on July 13, compared with a historical average of about 138 vessels per day. Tanker traffic was particularly limited: one tanker transit recorded July 12 and three on July 13. JMIC maintained its SEVERE threat assessment, citing 10 Iranian attacks since June 25. Attacks on three tankers on July 13 — including the Mombasa B and Al Bahyah on the southern Omani route — resulted in one fatality and multiple injuries.

The legal contradiction is threefold. Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated in late June that "no country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway — that's existing international law." Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wrote on May 28 that "all nations should reject outright any efforts by Iran to disrupt the free flow of commerce." The International Maritime Organization stated Monday that "there is no legal basis through which to introduce mandatory tolls simply to transit through a strait." By proposing the same toll mechanism the U.S. condemned Iran for, the administration has created a legal impossibility: any legal theory permitting one toll regime permits the other.

Iran's Foreign Minister Araghchi immediately exploited the contradiction, writing on social media: "POTUS is absolutely right... Iran has always been the GUARDIAN of the Strait and will remain so FOREVER. 20% is of course too much. We will be fair." The June 17 memorandum of understanding signed by Trump at Versailles explicitly prohibited Iran from imposing charges on commercial ships transiting the strait.
analysis:
The physical evidence is the JMIC traffic data: 4-12 transits per day versus the 138-vessel historical average. Trump's claim that "oil is flowing like never before" is contradicted by a shipping industry metric that tracks every vessel movement in real time. The JMIC data is more severe than the Kpler figures cited in prior coverage (14 vessels on July 12) — JMIC counted only 4, suggesting the actual transit count may be even lower than commercial tracking platforms report.

The legal paradox is structurally identical to the June 17 MOU violation framing: the U.S. cannot simultaneously argue that Iran's toll violates international law while imposing an identical mechanism on the same waterway. Rubio's own on-record statement — "no country is allowed to charge tolls or fees on an international waterway" — applies with equal force to the United States. The IMO's Monday statement closes the institutional loop: the UN body responsible for maritime law has explicitly stated there is no legal basis for mandatory transit tolls.

Hapag-Lloyd, one of the world's largest container shipping companies, stated that tolls are "fundamentally wrong" for international waterways — distinguishing Hormuz from the Suez Canal and Panama Canal, where infrastructure charges are justified by physical transit infrastructure. The estimated $32 million per-transit cost of a 20% toll makes the mechanism commercially unviable regardless of its legality. The shipping industry's on-record opposition creates a second institutional contradiction: the U.S. proposal is opposed not only by the UN maritime body but by the commercial entities it would apply to.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: Trump's 20% Hormuz toll proposal is contradicted by three independent institutional sources: his own Secretary of State (Rubio: "no country is allowed to charge tolls"), his own Treasury Secretary (Bessent: "all nations should reject"), and the International Maritime Organization ("no legal basis"). The JMIC traffic data — 4 transits on July 12 versus a 138-vessel daily average — shows the waterway is functionally shut down while Trump claims "oil is flowing like never before." Iran's Araghchi response inverts the framing: by adopting the U.S. language of guardianship and proposing to match the toll, Iran has converted the U.S. proposal into a bilateral symmetry that the June 17 MOU was designed to prevent. The $32 million per-transit cost ensures no commercial operator will pay it — the toll is a political declaration applied to a waterway that no longer functions as a commercial transit route.

documents_in_evidence: Rubio on-record statement on international waterway tolls
Bessent May 28 statement on commerce disruption
IMO Monday statement on legal basis for transit tolls
documents_absent: Full text of June 17 Versailles MOU
Hapag-Lloyd formal statement on Hormuz tolls
CENTCOM vessel tracking data (independent of JMIC)
Iranian naval traffic estimates for the same window
evidence_layers: JMIC real-time vessel count (4 transits vs 138 average)
Three on-record U.S. official statements contradicting the proposal
Iranian FM adoption of U.S. framing as inversion tactic
Shipping industry commercial viability assessment ($32M per transit)
telemetry.distinct_from_prior: prior coverage (July 13) focused on Kpler traffic data (14 vessels) and the Guardian declaration; this adds JMIC 4-transit data (more severe), three named U.S. official contradictions (Rubio, Bessent, IMO), Araghchi's inversion response, and Hapag-Lloyd's commercial viability assessment
